 A $500,000 Roth Portfolio Loaded With These Dividend Stocks Pays $34,350 a Year and the IRS Gets None of It
 Four dividend stocks sitting in the wrong account quietly hand a five-figure sum to the IRS every single year, and the bracket you land in determines exactly how much compounding power you surrender over time.
 By Chris Lange 
 Published October 24, 2026, 12:00pm ET · 3 min read

 Quick Read
 Holding HTGC and OHI in a taxable account at the 24% bracket costs $8,244 annually versus $0 in a Roth on the same $500,000 portfolio.
 NNN REIT just recorded its 37th consecutive annual dividend increase, with a conservative 69% AFFO payout ratio supporting continued growth.
 Reinvesting the annual Roth advantage at 4% compounds the gap to roughly $245,500 after 20 years, assuming no price gains or dividend growth.

 Take a hypothetical $500,000 split equally across four high-yield REITs and business development companies (BDCs). In the 24% federal bracket, that portfolio pays about $34,350 a year in dividends, and roughly $8,244 goes to the IRS. In 2026, the 24% bracket starts at $105,700 of taxable income for single filers and $211,400 for joint filers.
 Same Four Stocks, $8,244 a Year Apart
 REIT and BDC payouts are generally ordinary dividends. That means they’re taxed at your marginal rate instead of the 0%, 15%, or 20% rates that apply to qualified dividends, which makes them the most expensive income to hold in a brokerage account. The model below assumes a hypothetical $125,000 in each stock.

 In a Roth, you keep the full $34,350. In a taxable account, net income falls to $26,106. Over 10 years, assuming no growth and no new contributions, the gap adds up to $82,440.
 Hercules Capital: 9.83% Yield
 Hercules Capital ( NYSE:HTGC ) lends to venture-backed companies. It has the biggest tax bill in the group. Second-quarter net investment income of $92.9 million covered the base distribution 125% of the way, and trailing diluted EPS of $2.01 exceeds the $1.60 annual dividend.
 Omega Healthcare Investors: 6.05% Yield
 Omega Healthcare Investors ( NYSE:OHI ), a skilled nursing landlord, raised its quarterly dividend to $0.68. It also raised 2026 AFFO guidance to $3.22-$3.26 per share, well above its $2.69 annual payout. Management linked the raise to operator coverage, noting “there aren’t problems on the watch list.”
 NNN REIT: 5.89% Yield
 Triple-net retail properties are owned by NNN REIT ( NYSE:NNN ). It just posted its 37th consecutive annual dividend increase, and the new $0.62 quarterly rate yields a 69% AFFO payout ratio. A long record of dividend increases means decades of rising ordinary income, which a Roth shields from tax.
 Main Street Capital: 5.71% Yield
 Main Street Capital ( NYSE:MAIN | MAIN Price Prediction ) pays monthly dividends plus quarterly supplementals. The $0.30 September supplemental was its 20th in a row. In a brokerage account, every one of those payments is taxable. Second-quarter distributable net investment income before taxes came in at $1.08 per share, and trailing diluted EPS of $4.98 is above the $3.09 annual dividend.

 A top-bracket filer gives up $12,710 a year on the same portfolio. Joint filers reach the 32% bracket at $403,550 and the 37% bracket at $768,700. The higher your bracket, the more important the placement decision becomes.
 Compounding Turns $8,244 Into a Six-Figure Cost.
 Money paid in tax each year can’t be reinvested, and for high-yield payers, that lost reinvestment adds up faster. Reinvest the $8,244 annual Roth advantage at an assumed 4% rate, and the gap grows to about $99,000 after 10 years and roughly $245,500 after 20 years. Those figures assume no price gains and no dividend growth. Think of them as the permanent cost of holding these four stocks outside a Roth at the 24% bracket (the low-tax years before RMDs begin are the cheapest time to fix this, which is the whole subject of our free Roth Window guide ).
 Three Numbers to Run Before Tax Season
 Before December 31, add up the year-to-date distributions from every BDC or REIT in your taxable account and apply your marginal rate to the total. The result is your annual Roth delta.
 Plan out a phased Roth conversion , starting with your highest-yielding ordinary-dividend payer . Weigh the one-time conversion tax against the 20-year compounded figure above.
 Review how new Roth contributions, capped at $7,500 for 2026 ($8,600 if you’re 50 or older), would interact with ordinary-dividend payers versus qualified-dividend stocks, and discuss placement with a tax professional.
